lesson.title: Fiber Optic Cable: Sending Data as Light
lesson.summary: Fiber optic cable abandons electrical signaling altogether, sending data as pulses of light through a glass or plastic core, which sidesteps electromagnetic interference entirely and unlocks far higher bandwidth and longer reach than any copper medium.
lesson.body:
Twisted pair and coaxial cable, from the two previous chapters, both carry data as electrical signals on copper conductors, and both have to actively defend that electrical signal against electromagnetic interference, twisted pair through twisting geometry and coax through physical shielding. Fiber optic cable sidesteps the entire problem by not using electricity at all. Data travels as pulses of light through a thin strand of glass or plastic called the core, and because light is not an electrical phenomenon, a fiber strand is essentially immune to the electromagnetic interference that twisted pair and coax have to work so hard to resist, no twisting trick or shielding layer required to get that immunity.

The physics that keeps light traveling down the fiber rather than leaking out the sides is called total internal reflection. The core is surrounded by a layer called the cladding, made of a material with a slightly lower refractive index than the core itself. When light traveling through the core hits the boundary with the cladding at a shallow enough angle, instead of passing through and escaping, it reflects entirely back into the core, bouncing along the length of the fiber and staying confined to the path the fiber traces, even around gentle bends.

Fiber comes in two main varieties, distinguished mainly by core diameter. Multimode fiber has a relatively wide core, commonly around 50 or 62.5 microns, wide enough that light can travel down it along multiple distinct paths, or modes, simultaneously. Because those different paths travel slightly different distances, they arrive at slightly different times, a smearing effect called modal dispersion that limits how far multimode fiber can carry a signal before pulses blur into each other; it is the cheaper option, generally used with LED or lower cost laser sources over shorter runs such as within a building. Single-mode fiber has a much narrower core, typically around 9 microns, narrow enough that light can only travel one path straight down the center, eliminating modal dispersion entirely. Single-mode fiber supports dramatically longer distances and higher data rates as a result, at the cost of needing more precise, and more expensive, laser transmitters and tighter manufacturing tolerances, and it is the standard choice for long haul and backbone links.

Fiber's advantages compound with everything covered so far in this batch of chapters. Because it carries light rather than voltage, it needs no scheme to fight electromagnetic noise the way copper based NRZ or Manchester signaling sometimes does, though the underlying bit stream still has to be encoded as a pattern of light pulses, on for one signal state and off, or dimmer, for another, before it ever reaches the transmitter's laser or LED. Combined with its far higher usable bandwidth and much lower signal attenuation per kilometer than copper, fiber optic cable is what makes practical the extremely high channel capacities that the Shannon and Nyquist formulas from earlier chapters describe as theoretically available: a wide bandwidth, low noise medium like fiber pushes both terms of those capacity formulas in the right direction at once, which is exactly why fiber underlies the long distance backbone of essentially every large scale network in use today.
